title: Taking apart and rebuilding

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 26 Nov 2026 against NGSS 2-PS1-3 ('Make observations to construct an evidence-based account of how an object made of a small set of pieces can be disassembled and made into a new object'; clarification: pieces could include blocks, building bricks or other assorted small objects) and DCI PS1.A for grade 2 ('Different properties are suited to different purposes. A great variety of objects can be built up from a small set of pieces'), plus NC England Year 2 Uses of everyday materials and KS1 working scientifically. Every number was checked: the kit is 4 square blocks of 10 g and 2 planks twice as long at 20 g, so tower, pile and bridge all weigh 4 x 10 + 2 x 20 = 80 g; the bridge uses exactly the 4 squares as pillars and the 2 planks as the deck; a table (4 legs, 2-plank top) and a bench (2 blocks, 1 plank) fit the kit, a 4-wheel car and an 8-block tower do not. Wooden toy blocks of about 2.5 cm weigh roughly 8-10 g, so 10 g per block is realistic. Numeric items were checked at their range corners.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-years conservation and reassembly errors: pieces being 'used up' or lost when an object is taken apart (step 1 prediction 'Some get used up', the running Tower/Tray/Total count and the 'gone' slip); needing new pieces for a new object (step 2 prediction and the 'new' slip); judging weight by size or length, the classic non-conservation response in Piaget's conservation tasks (step 3 prediction 'Heavier: it is longer', disproved by three 80 g readings; the 'heavy' slip); believing the pieces themselves change (step 4 colour and material cards, the 'changed' slip); and thinking any kit can build anything (step 5 car and 8-block tower, the 'any' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is disassembly and reassembly of one fixed set of pieces: lifting a 6-piece tower apart top first into a tray with a live Tower/Tray/Total count, rebuilding the same pieces into a bridge slot by slot from the bottom up (a slot only takes its kind of piece and only once the space under it is filled), weighing tower, loose pile and bridge on one scale, sorting what changed from what stayed the same, and checking model requirements against the kit. It is not flagtwist (squashing one lump of clay), flagsolidbuild (naming composite 3-D solids) or any sorter-only lab; every task is about the same pieces in a new arrangement.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children see the total stay at 6 while the tower shrinks and the tray fills, then find that the very same pieces fill a bridge (with a toy car able to pass under it, a new job), then watch the scale read 80 g for all three forms. Sorting the six cards makes them state the pattern (shape and job change; number, colour, material and weight stay), and the kit check shows the limit: only models whose pieces you have. Each done message names what they found and the kid text confirms it.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Some get used up' (all 6 pieces arrive in the tray), 'No, a bridge needs new pieces' (the bridge is built from the tower's pieces with none left over) and 'Heavier: it is longer' (the bridge reads 80 g, the same as the tower and the pile). The reveal line names the child's prediction once the task is done.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; each wrong option carries a slip tag with its own message: 'gone' (nothing is used up, count the pieces), 'new' (no new pieces needed), 'heavy' (same pieces, same weight; a longer or lower shape adds no weight), 'changed' (the pieces do not change, only where they go) and 'any' (you can only build what your pieces allow). Lab steps also give specific replies, e.g. 'That space needs a square block, not a long plank' and 'Build from the bottom up. Fill the space under it first, or the piece would fall.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the kid (6.5) and adult (9.5) limits; the kid text scores around grade 0-1 with short sentences and familiar words (blocks, tower, bridge, weigh, same). Lab instructions are one short line each with a running count, pictures of real-looking wooden blocks carry the meaning, and the fig has the young class for 56 px buttons.

no_filler.evidence: Every sentence teaches part of the idea (taking apart keeps every piece, rebuilding uses the same pieces in a new way, shape and job change, number, material and weight stay, a kit limits what can be built) or checks it. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under the 12% similarity limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark themes and on desktop for every step before and after Show me. Two problems found on screenshots were fixed: tray planks overflowed the tray (pieces now sized to a quarter of the tray), and every loose piece in the build step had a selection outline (a -1 flag was truthy). Blocks were enlarged so the bridge and loose pieces are big enough to drag. Real pointer tests on iPhone 13: tapping a middle tower piece gives 'Take the top piece first', dragging the top piece to the tray gives 'Took off the green block. 1 in the tray, 5 left', dragging a plank to a block space gives 'That space needs a square block', and a block then fits.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('Take the green block off the top of the tower', 'Put a square block in the left pillar, bottom', 'Weigh the loose pile', 'The total weight goes in Stayed the same', 'Yes, our kit can build a table'), so dragging and tapping the canvas are optional. The canvas aria-label updates with every action, challenge feedback is a polite live region, colour is never the only cue (each block is also named, readings are numbers), and the browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations or console errors.

sources: NGSS Lead States (2013) Next Generation Science Standards, 2-PS1-3 Matter and Its Interactions, with clarification statement; DCI PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter (grade 2)
DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 2 Uses of everyday materials and Key Stage 1 Working scientifically
Piaget, J. and Inhelder, B. (1974) The Child's Construction of Quantities: Conservation and Atomism (conservation of substance and weight in young children)
